premises.text: (A1) The monitor and the anchor run outside the reach of the trust domain that holds the adversary; on Home Assistant they do when the core runs in an unprivileged container on its own bridge network with only its configuration directory mounted, which the documented \texttt{--privileged} host-network command does not provide (Section~\ref{sec:bg}).
(A2) Only the monitor and the anchor hold the HMAC key of the authenticated append path; because the shipped add-on manifest provisions no key, the key is provisioned by hand.
(A3) SHA-256 is collision resistant and the node encoding is injective, so two rows that differ in a covered field have different node hashes.

(A4) In the evaluated runs the anchor host is trusted: their anchor kept its records with no hash link between them and published its head only on the same host, so their first anchored roots are only as reliable as that host.
(G1) Detection: a rewrite or deletion of a covered row after its segment is sealed changes that segment's recomputed root, which then differs from its first anchored root at one-second granularity.

(G2) Localization: after a violation the investigator receives a quarantine that contains every tampered element of the sealed segments and leaves the committed attribution of every row outside it usable.
Covered evidence is a row that is present in the activity record when the monitor seals its segment.

Any rewrite or deletion of such a row after its segment is sealed is detected at one-second granularity, relative to the segment's first anchored root, which in the evaluated runs the verifier takes on the anchor host's word (A4).

Taking violated segments innermost first and skipping coarser ones that contain a quarantined finer one keeps every tampered element of a sealed segment quarantined, at the finest granularity the roots distinguish, provided the anchor's record of sealed segments is complete (A4).
A per-poll keylog also commits each row's fields when the monitor first reads it, which catches a row created earlier and moved into sealed time.

Under coverage the verifier recomputes each sealed segment over the rows up to the anchored highest keys, so added rows never make a violation ambiguous, and a row found in sealed time over 30 s after its timestamp is attributable.

A marker must be tagged under a separate operator key held outside the hub's trust domain, since an integration can itself call the purge service and emit events, and the anchor refuses one under the append key.

evasion_conditions.condition: the rewritten input is not committed
evasion_conditions.cases: a scheme that omits the column (row scheme: user column, old_state_id, last_changed_ts); the name map and entity registry without the name-map digest; automation traces

statement.text: The displayed cause also reads the name map and the entity registry, which an integration can change for committed rows without editing them, and the monitor commits these inputs only with its optional name-map digest (Section~\ref{sec:des}).

The automation traces with which an admin viewer can expose laundering lie outside the covered evidence: the hub process keeps them in memory and in its configuration directory, which the monitor does not commit, so that cross-check is not tamper-evident under the guarantee.
With the same harness and anchor, the row-scheme monitor detected none of 90 random-id swaps, and the row scheme recomputed offline none of 90 member-account swaps, since it omits the user column.

evasion_conditions.bound: the renderer closure measured on the release (stable columns cover every column the output reads)

evasion_conditions.condition: the row is changed or deleted before any poll reads it

statement.text: A row changed or deleted before any poll of the monitor reads it is never committed, and the observation window is the bound that the monitor's polling, once per observation interval, places on the guarantee.
With the monitor reading a local read-only mount, a row escapes commitment with probability 0.98 when it is deleted 1~s after its write, 0.27 after 5~s and 0.012 after 10~s.

evasion_conditions.bound: measured window (median 3.8 s write to anchor; escape probability 0.98 / 0.27 / 0.012 at 1 / 5 / 10 s); does not apply to rows committed before the adversary's code arrived (SI-S096-07)

evasion_conditions.condition: the row is forged when first written by resident code

statement.text: Write-time forgery therefore stays outside the guarantee whatever the commitment covers, and a resident adversary that misattributes its own actuations this way escapes detection (Section~\ref{sec:eval-write-time-forgery}).
After the late-row test neither monitor detected any strategy at one-second granularity, 0 of 30 trials each.

evasion_conditions.bound: none: no earlier committed version exists

evasion_conditions.condition: a row inserted into sealed time with a timestamp within LATE_BOUND (30 s) of the copies that lacked it
evasion_conditions.cases: backdating by less than about 35 s passes as a benign late row

statement.text: Rows inserted into sealed time are attributable, whether into an edited second or into time that held no row, because each anchored record names the highest row key and the time it sealed through and the monitor commits each row when it first reads it; a row backdated by less than about 35 s passes as a late commit (Section~\ref{sec:des}).
Coverage passes a row backdated by less than about 35 s as a late commit, and the evaluated escrow held no row that reached the recorder after its second was sealed.

Under coverage the verifier recomputes each sealed segment over the rows up to the anchored highest keys, so added rows never make a violation ambiguous, and a row found in sealed time over 30 s after its timestamp is attributable.

evasion_conditions.bound: LATE_BOUND = 30 s plus one poll; the keylog catches rows created earlier and moved in (SI-S032-10)

evasion_conditions.condition: a deletion that a lifecycle marker excuses
evasion_conditions.cases: a purge-shaped deletion confined to rows older than the scoped cutoff; a marker declaring the deletion's own cutoff

statement.text: Purges also bound the guarantee: by default Home Assistant deletes rows older than ten days every night~\cite{harecorder}, and any integration, the adversary's included, can call the same purge service, so a purge is excused only when a marker from outside the hub declares it, and a purge-shaped deletion escaped in 4 of 4 generated deployments at the cost of about half the recorded history (Appendix~\ref{sec:appe}).
The eleventh case, a purge-shaped deletion, escaped detection in 4 of 4 generated deployments at the cost of deleting 0.498 to 0.520 of the recorded history.
Markers declaring each deletion's own cutoff excused all of them.

A marker must be tagged under a separate operator key held outside the hub's trust domain, since an integration can itself call the purge service and emit events, and the anchor refuses one under the append key.

evasion_conditions.bound: markers need the operator key outside the hub; the purge-shaped deletion costs about half the history (0.498-0.520 of it on generated deployments)

evasion_conditions.cases: the monitor could not read a consistent copy

statement.text: An evidence-unobservable record carries no segment root, so the verifier compares nothing for its interval and its rows are not covered evidence.

evasion_conditions.bound: the interval is anchored and reported

evasion_conditions.condition: the anchor host rewrites or withholds records

statement.text: (A4) In the evaluated runs the anchor host is trusted: their anchor kept its records with no hash link between them and published its head only on the same host, so their first anchored roots are only as reliable as that host.
A rewrite, reorder, deletion or truncation by the anchor host is thus detected up to the latest witnessed head, but the evaluated guarantee still assumes (A4).

evasion_conditions.bound: linked anchor and witness detect a rewrite up to the latest witnessed head; the evaluated guarantee assumes (A4)

evasion_conditions.condition: two rows that differ in a covered field share a node hash

statement.text: (A3) SHA-256 is collision resistant and the node encoding is injective, so two rows that differ in a covered field have different node hashes.

The first fourteen evaluated runs used an earlier encoding that joined the fields with a separator byte, under which 7.33\% [7.28, 7.38] of 1,090,765 recorder rows admit a splice that keeps the node hash.

evasion_conditions.bound: typed encoding injective; under the earlier encoding 7.33% of 1,090,765 rows admitted a splice (measured)

evasion_conditions.condition: the monitor or anchor is within the adversary's reach, or the append key leaks
evasion_conditions.cases: (A1), (A2): privileged core or host network on the same host

statement.text: (A1) The monitor and the anchor run outside the reach of the trust domain that holds the adversary; on Home Assistant they do when the core runs in an unprivileged container on its own bridge network with only its configuration directory mounted, which the documented \texttt{--privileged} host-network command does not provide (Section~\ref{sec:bg}).
(A2) Only the monitor and the anchor hold the HMAC key of the authenticated append path; because the shipped add-on manifest provisions no key, the key is provisioned by hand.

The deployment boundary is (A1): a privileged container holds every capability and the host's devices~\cite{dockerrun}, so with the core privileged or on the host network, as under the documented Container command and on Home Assistant OS and Supervised installs, the monitor and the anchor lie within the adversary's reach on the same host, and the guarantee then needs them on another host.
